title: [A2 • Band 4.0] Bài 117: The Dodo: Re-evaluating an Extinct Icon
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 117 (LEVEL A2 • BAND 4.0)

The Dodo: Re-evaluating an Extinct Icon

Paragraph 1. For three hundred years, old stories painted the dodo as a fat, clumsy, and silly bird that died out because it was weak. However, modern scientists used bone scans and new studies to prove that this old picture is wrong. In truth, the dodo was a strong, fast runner that fit its island home very well.

Paragraph 2. The dodo lived only on Mauritius, a tropical island in the Indian Ocean. Millions of years ago, fruit-eating pigeons flew to this island. Because there were no meat-eating land animals there, the birds stopped flying to save energy and lived on the ground. They grew strong legs and big hooked beaks to crack hard forest nuts and bite enemies. Their brains were as smart as modern pigeons, with a strong sense of smell to find ripe fruit on the forest floor.

Paragraph 3. Everything changed in 1598 when Dutch sailors landed on Mauritius. Having never seen dangerous land animals, dodos showed zero fear. Instead of running away, they stood still, so sailors caught them easily with bare hands. Still, sailors disliked eating the dodo because its meat was tough and oily.

Paragraph 4. The real killer of the dodo was not human hunting, but new animals brought on European ships. Settlers brought pigs, black rats, and monkeys onto the island. Because dodos built simple nests on the ground and laid only one egg each time, hungry pigs and rats easily broke the eggs and ate baby birds. By 1681, the last dodo died out. Almost two centuries later, in 1865, a teacher named George Clark dug thousands of dodo bones from a wet swamp, helping modern science rebuild how the real bird looked.
